name: Nasal testosterone (Natesto)

lead: Natesto is a prescription testosterone gel given through the nose for men with low testosterone. People on TRT discuss it because small studies suggest it may keep sperm production and gonadotropins more intact than other testosterone forms.

The appearance link is the usual TRT one: restored testosterone supports muscle and lower fat. Trials in hypogonadal men report normalised testosterone, and several small studies report preserved semen parameters. A 90-day trial of 306 hypogonadal men found the nasal gel normalised androgen levels, with extensions to one year. These studies are in medical patients, not cosmetic users.

paras: It is short-acting, so it is applied several times a day under a prescriber's direction. It suits people who want an alternative to skin gels or injections and who care about fertility.

As with other testosterone products, reported concerns include raised hematocrit, blood pressure monitoring, acne, and prostate and cardiovascular questions. It is a controlled prescription drug and is banned in competitive sport.

angle.text: Natesto is a prescription nasal testosterone for diagnosed low T, popular in TRT circles because small studies suggest it may keep sperm production more intact. The looks link is the usual TRT one, more muscle and less fat, studied in hypogonadal men.

lead: Natesto is a prescription testosterone nasal gel used for testosterone replacement in men with hypogonadism. Wikipedia lists it as the intranasal testosterone product, supplied as a metered spray.[1]

In a 90-day randomised, open-label, dose-ranging study of 306 hypogonadal men, the nasal gel normalised androgen levels, with extensions to one year.[2] It is discussed in muscle and hormone communities mainly as a short-acting option that, in several small studies, did not suppress gonadotropins or sperm in the way other testosterone forms can.[3][4]
infobox: Testosterone first approved for medical use
Rx-only; testosterone is US Schedule III

paras: Natesto's use is testosterone replacement in hypogonadal men.[2] Stratified analysis of a phase 3 study examined efficacy by baseline testosterone, comparing testosterone, LH, FSH, erectile function, mood and lean body mass across groups.[5] Another study examined patients with seasonal allergies.[6]

Testosterone products as a class can cause acne, breast enlargement, raised hematocrit, worsened sleep apnea and, with prolonged use, reduced sperm production, and are contraindicated in pregnancy.[1] A cross-sectional comparison examined secondary polycythemia in men on nasal gel versus intramuscular testosterone cypionate.[7] A registered study was planned to monitor ambulatory blood pressure in men on the nasal gel.[8] Advantages cited in the initial study include ease of administration, low dose and no risk of secondary transference to others.[2]
The gel is delivered into the nasal cavity, giving short-acting testosterone exposure.[2][3] A study of its effects on doping markers examined intranasal delivery.[9]

Testosterone is a controlled substance in many countries, available only by prescription in most, and banned in competitive sport by the World Anti-Doping Agency.[1] A patient-preference study compared topical and nasal testosterone satisfaction.[10]

In the 306-man dose-ranging study, nasal gel normalised testosterone in hypogonadal men.[2] A University of Miami single-arm trial evaluated effects on reproductive hormones, semen parameters, quality of life and sexual function, and an earlier report of the ongoing trial described maintained FSH, LH and semen parameters.[3][4] Small studies reported spermatogenesis resuming after switching from long-acting testosterone, and improved libido with maintained semen parameters and reduced estradiol after switching from clomiphene.[11][12] Registered trials include a 60-participant semen study and a blood pressure study.[8][13]
